item.title: Review of “지정학 경쟁 시대, 한국의 원전 외교: 체코 원전 수주 사례” [South Korea’s nuclear energy diplomacy in an era of geopolitical competition: Insights from the Czech nuclear power plant case]
item.body:
# Article reviewed

Article / author / journal: Hanna Lee (이한나), 한국과 국제사회 9(5), 2025, pp. 1149-1176
DOI or source URL: https://doi.org/10.22718/kga.2025.9.5.041

This article examines how South Korea’s nuclear power exports are shaped by its asymmetric alliance with the United States, using the Czech nuclear project won in 2025 as its case (pp. 1149, 1152). US–China rivalry has spread to advanced technology, and the United States now treats nuclear power as a strategic asset and as a means of drawing allies into its network (pp. 1150-1151). The question is what constraints a smaller ally faces in such an industry and how it responds (p. 1151).

To answer this question, the author draws on James Morrow’s autonomy-security exchange model, in which the weaker partner in an alliance gains security by accepting the stronger partner’s requests and gives up part of its autonomy in return (pp. 1154-1155). In strategic industries, refusing a request from the stronger ally may cost the weaker state both the benefits of the industry and the security it already has (p. 1155). A smaller ally can refuse, which may lead to decoupling, or accept, either by bandwagoning (following the stronger ally’s lead) or by balancing in a limited way to widen its room for autonomy. These options draw on an earlier study of how small and medium states respond to security threats (pp. 1156-1159).

The growth of Korea’s nuclear industry is traced from the first cooperation agreement with the United States in the 1950s to the export of a nuclear power plant to the United Arab Emirates in 2009 (pp. 1159-1161). This growth took place under the Korea–US nuclear agreement and a technology usage agreement with Westinghouse, which meant paying usage fees and accepting US regulation while working towards technological self-reliance (p. 1161).

Korea won the Dukovany contract, signed in 2025 as its second nuclear export after the United Arab Emirates (p. 1162). After the EU and NATO recommended excluding China and Russia from nuclear projects for security reasons, the Czech government left them out of the 2021 tender and began screening bids from Korea, the United States and France (pp. 1163, 1166). Korea faced an intellectual property dispute with Westinghouse, settled in January 2025 through a memorandum of understanding with the US government and a global agreement with the company (pp. 1151, 1164, 1166). Press reports discussed in the study indicate that the settlement included a long-term technology usage fee and limits on the regions where Korea can bid, although the full agreement has not been published (pp. 1151, 1164-1165).

Korea accepted US conditions to win the contract and gave up a considerable part of its technical and policy autonomy, while gaining steadier cooperation with the United States, room to seek new export opportunities outside the restricted regions and an expected gain in the stability of its fuel supply (pp. 1166-1167). The author describes this as a choice close to bandwagoning and suggests that Korea look for ways to widen its autonomy in future negotiations (p. 1167).

**A single export contract offers a view of how an alliance works in practice, and Morrow’s model gives a clear way to follow what Korea accepted and what it gained in return.** The same question can be followed in other strategic industries, such as semiconductors, batteries and AI, mentioned at the end of the study (p. 1169).
item.author: Ines Amrouche
item.summary: This review introduces a study of how South Korea's nuclear power exports are shaped by its asymmetric alliance with the United States, using the Czech nuclear project won in 2025 as a case.
